Oven
UV-en
noun
Old English ofen, cognate with the German Ofen and Latin-related forms for a baking vessel; in Scripture usually the portable clay jar or the domed floor-hearth heated with grass, thorns, and stubble.

Biblical Definition

The oven of Scripture is not the iron range but a clay vessel or domed hearth, heated fiercely with grass, thorns, and dung, and then swept out for the cakes to be slapped upon its inner wall. Because it was fired with whatever the field yielded, our Lord could reason from it: “if God so clothe the grass of the field, which to day is, and to morrow is cast into the oven, shall he not much more clothe you, O ye of little faith?” (Mat 6:30). The oven appears in the law of the offerings, where the meat offering baken in the oven is the portion passed through the fire (Lev 2:4), and in the law of cleanness, where an oven touched by a carcase must be broken down (Lev 11:35). But its great use is as the standing figure of the wrath of God. “Thou shalt make them as a fiery oven in the time of thine anger” (Psa 21:9); and Malachi closes the Old Testament with it: “the day cometh, that shall burn as an oven; and all the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly, shall be stubble” (Mal 4:1). Hosea turns the same image inward upon the heart: the conspirators of Israel “have made ready their heart like an oven,” banked overnight and bursting into flame in the morning (Hos 7:6). The oven is thus the whole compass of the word — the fire that bakes the offering, the fire that consumes the stubble, and the fire that smoulders in a man’s own bosom until it breaks out.

Webster 1828 Definition

A place built of clay or stone, arched over and heated for baking; in Scripture a standing figure of the wrath of God and of the smouldering heart.

OVEN, an arched cavity or place built of stone or brick, and heated for baking bread or other victuals.

Old English ofen; German Ofen. In the East, a portable clay jar or a domed floor-hearth.

Heated with grass, thorns, and stubble — whence the Lord’s argument from the grass (Mat 6:30).

The meat offering baken in the oven (Lev 2:4); an oven defiled must be broken down (Lev 11:35).

Figuratively, the day of the LORD burning as an oven (Mal 4:1; Psa 21:9).

Key Scripture

Mal 4:1 — "For, behold, the day cometh, that shall burn as an oven; and all the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly, shall be stubble: and the day that cometh shall burn them up, saith the LORD of hosts, that it shall leave them neither root nor branch."

Psa 21:9 — "Thou shalt make them as a fiery oven in the time of thine anger: the LORD shall swallow them up in his wrath, and the fire shall devour them."

Mat 6:30 — "Wherefore, if God so clothe the grass of the field, which to day is, and to morrow is cast into the oven, shall he not much more clothe you, O ye of little faith?"

Hos 7:6 — "For they have made ready their heart like an oven, whiles they lie in wait: their baker sleepeth all the night; in the morning it burneth as a flaming fire."

Modern Corruption

Malachi’s oven is seized by annihilationism as proof that the wicked are simply burned out of existence — a reading the figure will not carry and the Lord Himself forbids.

expand to see more

The corruption is exegetical and it is popular: because the proud are called stubble and the day burns as an oven leaving neither root nor branch, the conclusion is drawn that the punishment of the lost is extinction — a swift consuming and then nothing. Edward Fudge’s conditionalism and the annihilationism now common in broad evangelicalism rest heavily on such fuel-and-fire language. But a figure must be read by the plain teaching it illustrates, not made to overthrow it. The same Lord who spoke of the oven spoke of the fire that is not quenched and the worm that dieth not (Mar 9:44), of everlasting punishment set in the very same sentence and the very same word as life eternal (Mat 25:46), and of the smoke of their torment ascending up for ever and ever, having no rest day nor night (Rev 14:11). Stubble language describes the helplessness of the wicked before the fire, not the duration of their suffering; and the eternity of the punishment follows necessarily from the infinite worth of the God against whom the offence is committed. To read the oven as extinction is to comfort the impenitent with a sentence God never passed.

Recover what the oven is actually for. It burns two ways in Scripture, and the difference is everything. In Lev 2:4 the fire receives the offering — fine flour, mingled with oil, unleavened, passed through the heat and accepted; and that oven is a shadow of Christ, who went into the fire of the Father’s wrath in the room of His people and came out the acceptable offering. In Mal 4:1 the fire receives the stubble. Every soul stands in one relation or the other, and there is no third. Then observe the tenderness of Mat 6:30, where the very same oven becomes an argument for peace: God arrays the grass gorgeously though it is fuel by tomorrow — how much more will He clothe the children He has bought? And Hosea’s word searches the professor: a heart made ready like an oven, banked all night while the baker sleeps, bursting out in the morning. Sin does not need tending to grow hot. Let a man ask what his own heart has been smouldering over while he slept.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The clay baking-jar or hearth of the East; the standing emblem of the day of the LORD, and of the offering passed through fire.

expand to see more

Oven — Old English ofen; German Ofen, a baking vessel.

Hebrew tannur, the portable clay oven (Lev 2:4; Hos 7:4; Mal 4:1).

Greek klibanos, the earthen baking-jar (Mat 6:30; Luk 12:28).

Fuelled with grass, thorns, and stubble — the ground of the Lord’s argument for providence.

Two ovens in Scripture: the one that bakes the offering, the one that burns the stubble.

Usage

"The day that shall burn as an oven leaves the proud neither root nor branch."

"The grass that fuels tomorrow’s oven is clothed today — how much more shall He clothe you?"

"A heart made ready like an oven burns in the morning; sin smoulders while the baker sleeps."
